aspects.says: ArrayList is preferred over LinkedList in almost all cases, for its cache-friendly contiguous array, O(1) index access and smaller per-element memory.
ConcurrentHashMap offers forEach, search and reduce bulk operations with a parallelism threshold.
aspects.reason: the threshold changes only how the work is split; the answer is the same as a plain loop's, so no test can tell whether the reader used it

aspects.says: Since Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap locks a single bin per update and uses CAS for empty bins, so threads updating different bins do not wait for each other.
ConcurrentHashMap refuses null keys and values so that get returning null always means absent, and a null value must be stored as a sentinel.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: CopyOnWriteArrayList suits a listener registry: addIfAbsent refuses duplicates and notification iterates a snapshot that a listener may change without breaking it.
Every CopyOnWriteArrayList write copies the whole array, which makes it a poor fit for write-heavy work.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a cost claim no deterministic test can observe; the choice it drives, CopyOnWriteArrayList against a synchronized list, is asked in page 6.5.2's quiz

aspects.says: LinkedList and ArrayDeque serve as a Deque with constant-time adds and removals at both ends, and poll and peek return null on an empty deque.
HashMap is an array of buckets indexed by hash & (capacity - 1), whose collision chains turn into red-black trees past eight nodes.
aspects.reason: bucket indexing and capacity are the subject of page 6.5.4, practised there in the buckets practice; the tree-bin switch is internal and invisible through the Map API

aspects.says: HashMap accepts one null key and null values, and containsKey tells an absent key from one mapped to null.
aspects.reason: the single-threaded contrast the nullable practice starts from; the practice's own tests check a stored null against an absent key

aspects.says: A HashSet does not keep insertion order; an ordered set such as LinkedHashSet keeps the order elements were first added.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: No non-concurrent collection is thread-safe by default.
aspects.reason: the subject of page 6.5.2, whose counter and iteration practices check it

aspects.says: Pre-sizing a collection whose size is known avoids resizing.
aspects.reason: the subject of page 6.5.4, practised there in the resizes practice

aspects.says: Java 21 adds SequencedCollection, and List.of, Set.of and Map.of make unmodifiable collections.
aspects.reason: API notes the page lists without teaching; minor, not practised

aspects.says: A set refuses an element equal to one it already holds, comparing by equals and hashCode rather than by identity.

aspects.reason: the same null rule as ConcurrentHashMap, which the nullable practice already checks

aspects.says: ConcurrentSkipListSet keeps its elements sorted and answers first, last and range queries whose bounds can be inclusive, returning views backed by the set.
Non-concurrent collections have fail-fast iterators; concurrent ones have weakly consistent iterators.
aspects.reason: the subject of page 6.5.3, whose snapshots and removal practices check it
